content: Corneal abrasion is a frequently encountered condition by ophthalmologists, emergency physicians, and primary care providers. One of the treatment options for managing corneal abrasions involves the use of ocular antibiotics. However, there is currently no comprehensive synthesis of evidence regarding the use of antibiotic prophylaxis in traumatic corneal abrasions. This review was conducted to evaluate the existing evidence on this topic. The primary objective of this review was to assess the safety and efficacy of topical antibiotic prophylaxis following corneal abrasion. Specifically, the review aimed to investigate two key outcomes: (1) the incidence of infection when comparing antibiotics to placebo or alternative antibiotics, and (2) the time to clinical cure, defined as complete epithelial healing, when comparing antibiotics to placebo or alternative antibiotics. To gather relevant data, a systematic search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), Ovid MEDLINE, Embase, PubMed, LILACS, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (ICTRP). No restrictions were applied regarding the date or language of the studies. The last search was performed on April 25, 2021. The inclusion criteria for this review were randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared antibiotics with either another antibiotic or placebo in children and adults with corneal abrasions caused by any etiology. Standard Cochrane methodology was employed, and the certainty of the evidence was assessed using the GRADE classification. The search yielded 8,661 records, of which 7,690 titles and abstracts were screened after removing duplicates. Thirty-two full-text reports were reviewed, and two studies were ultimately included in the analysis. These two studies involved a total of 527 eyes from 527 participants. One study was conducted in Denmark, and the other in India. However, neither study addressed most of the prespecified primary and secondary outcomes. The first study, conducted in Denmark, was a parallel-group RCT that compared chloramphenicol ocular ointment with fusidic acid ocular gel. The frequency of application was not clearly reported. This study included 153 participants aged over 5 years with corneal abrasions and had a follow-up duration of one day. No participants in the fusidic acid group developed secondary infections, while three participants (4.1%) in the chloramphenicol group experienced a mild reaction (risk ratio [RR] 0.15, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.01 to 2.79; 144 participants; very low certainty evidence). By day 1, 31 participants (44.3%) in the fusidic acid group and 34 participants (46.6%) in the chloramphenicol group were considered cured, defined as having no infection and complete resolution of the abrasion (RR 0.94, 95% CI 0.65 to 1.34; 144 participants; very low certainty evidence). The study did not provide specific data on pain levels but reported that pain was not influenced by the interventions. The most common adverse events were itching and discomfort, which occurred in approximately one-third of participants in both groups (low certainty evidence). The second study, conducted in India, was a multicenter, two-arm RCT that enrolled 374 participants aged over 5 years with corneal abrasions presenting within 48 hours of injury. This study compared a three-day course of chloramphenicol-clotrimazole ocular ointment with chloramphenicol-placebo ointment, both administered three times daily. By day 3, all 169 participants (100%) in the chloramphenicol-clotrimazole group and 203 out of 205 participants (99%) in the chloramphenicol-placebo group were cured, defined as complete epithelialization of the cornea without evidence of infection (RR 1.01, 95% CI 0.99 to 1.03; 374 participants; very low certainty evidence). Four participants in the chloramphenicol-placebo group experienced mild adverse events, including mild chemosis and irritation in two participants (1%) and small sterile corneal infiltrates in another two participants (1%) (low certainty evidence). In conclusion, the available evidence regarding the use of antibiotic prophylaxis for corneal abrasions is of low to very low certainty. As a result, the potential benefits of antibiotics in preventing ocular infections or accelerating epithelial healing remain unclear. Furthermore, there is insufficient evidence to determine whether any specific antibiotic regimen is superior to another. There is a pressing need for well-designed RCTs to evaluate the efficacy and safety of ocular antibiotics in treating corneal abrasions, particularly in high-risk populations and with a focus on the formulation of interventions.
